pros.title: traditional kefir grains are tiny microbe communities
pros.explanation: They are reusable clusters of bacteria and yeast, not cereal grains.

pros.title: fermentation can make lactose easier to handle
pros.explanation: A small human study found plain kefir was better tolerated than milk by adults who struggle to digest lactose.

pros.title: the drinkable format is genuinely handy
pros.explanation: Have it straight from the fridge, blend it into a smoothie, or use it as a tangy base for dressings.

cons.title: sweetened bottles can change the whole deal
cons.explanation: Added sugar can turn a useful fermented drink into something much closer to a liquid dessert.

cons.title: milk allergy is still a hard stop
cons.explanation: Fermentation can change the lactose, but it does not remove the milk proteins that trigger an allergy.

cons.title: the sour, slightly funky flavour is not for everyone
cons.explanation: Plain kefir tastes much tangier than ordinary milk or sweetened yogurt.

scoreReadiness.summary: Exact USDA low-fat plain-kefir identity with per-100g nutrient values, a published glycemic-index result, explicit display estimates, and source-backed fermentation context.
caveats: Kefir varies by milk-fat level, brand, starter culture, flavouring, and added sugar; this entry represents the named USDA low-fat plain identity.
Sugar and protein-quality display rows use labelled estimates where the exact USDA record does not expose the required FoodRanked metric.

sourceNotes: Production source pass for ready-to-drink low-fat plain kefir.
All displayed nutrition values use a per-100g basis.
Primary nutrient identity is USDA FoodData Central FDC 170904.
Glycemic index uses a small human crossover study of Lifeway low-fat plain kefir.
Protein-quality rows are labelled FoodRanked display estimates, not USDA nutrient measurements.
